Dear Bidisha,

You asked how the Bangalore question ended up. Short answer: better than I feared. My husband and I had been circling each other for two weeks over the job offer, so one evening we each took a sheet of paper and wrote our top three priorities separately, no peeking. Mine: career growth, being near my mother, and enough savings. His, when we swapped: his own work, his parents nearby, and money. I laughed, because it was practically the same list with different names on it. We had been arguing about the city when what we both wanted was growth, family and security. We have not decided yet, but the fight has gone out of it. Come and visit soon.

Sabina 🙂

Shreya, you asked how Nitesh and I didn't end up divorced over the Hyderabad offer. Honestly, it was two sheets of paper.
We'd been fighting for a week. He wanted to take the job; I wanted to stay near my parents in Nagpur. Every conversation went in circles.
Then one night I said, "Let's stop talking. Each of us writes, alone, what matters most. Then we swap."
I wrote: my parents are getting older; I want to keep growing at work; I don't want us to struggle with money. He wrote: a real step up in his career; staying close to both families; not being stretched thin financially.
We swapped. We read. We just sat there.
Family was on both lists. Money was on both lists. Growth was on both lists. We'd been arguing like enemies when we wanted the same things, just in a different order.
I'm Vandana, and I'm stubborn. But that night even I laughed.

How did Vandana feel after reading Nitesh's list?
qa.a: Vandana felt surprised and relieved, even laughing, on seeing that they wanted the same things in a different order.

qa.a: They could look at options that serve all three values, such as a trial period or regular visits to Nagpur, and weigh them together.

qa.q: How might Nitesh have felt when they swapped lists?
qa.a: Nitesh likely felt understood and less defensive, seeing that Vandana also cared about growth and money, not only staying put.

grounding: It shows a couple facing a job offer in another city each writing what matters most, and discovering shared values beneath the disagreement.

I'm Yusuf. Vikas and I share a cabin at the pharma company in Vadodara, so I heard bits of this over two weeks.
Vikas had an offer from our Bengaluru office. His wife, Farida, runs a small tuition centre here, and her parents are two streets away. At first he'd come in looking like he hadn't slept, muttering about how "impossible" it was.
Then one Monday he showed me a folded paper. "We wrote separate lists last night," he said. "What matters most to each of us."
He didn't show me hers, but he told me what surprised him. They both wrote family. They both wrote financial security. And Farida had written that she wanted him to grow, and that she was proud of the offer.
He looked different after that. Less trapped. I don't know what they decided in the end, but he stopped calling it impossible.

qa.q: Where does Farida run her tuition centre?
qa.a: In Vadodara, where she runs a small tuition centre.

qa.q: How did Vikas seem to feel after the lists, compared with before?
qa.a: Before, Vikas seemed sleepless and trapped; after, he seemed lighter and more hopeful, no longer calling it impossible.

qa.q: What else could Vikas and Farida do with their lists?
qa.a: They could compare options like moving, staying or a trial against the values they share, and decide together.

qa.q: How might Farida see the offer, based on what she wrote?
qa.a: Farida seems proud of Vikas and wants him to grow, even while caring about her work and her parents nearby.

grounding: It shows, through a colleague's account, a couple facing a job offer in another city writing their priorities separately and finding shared values beneath the disagreement.
